name: Eyebrow microblading
lead: Microblading is a semi-permanent cosmetic tattooing technique in which a technician uses a handheld tool with fine blades or needles to draw hair-like strokes of pigment into the upper dermis of the eyebrows. It is used to fill sparse, thin or uneven brows, to reshape them, and to disguise brow loss, giving a fuller and more defined brow line that does not need daily pencilling.[1][2][3]

Wikipedia reports that results can last up to about two years, with a touch-up recommended around six weeks later and then every 12 to 18 months.[2] It is also known as eyebrow embroidery, feathering, microstroking, 3D brows or nanoblading, and it is performed in clinics and beauty studios.[2] Published clinical literature consists largely of narrative reviews, a cross-sectional awareness survey, laser-removal series, and case reports of complications, including granulomatous reactions, sarcoidosis, allergic contact dermatitis, cellulitis and a reported mpox transmission.[4][5][6][7][8][9][10][11][12]

In looksmaxxing forums, microblading is discussed by men who want thicker, darker brows, with opinions that range from favourable to critical of how natural the results look, and with alternatives such as minoxidil often raised in the same threads.[14][15][16]

paras: Microblading is described as a form of superficial micropigmentation in which pigment is deposited as far as the papillary dermis with a manual tool, unlike machine tattooing where a motorised needle is used.[1][2][17] Because the pigment sits in the upper dermis, it fades faster than traditional tattoos.[2] A review in Current Problems in Dermatology describes the method as one in which tiny cuts in the outer skin are filled with dark pigment to simulate a natural hair.[3]

Eyebrow shape is usually planned first. A 2021 review lists the parts of the brow as head, body, arch and tail, says shape should suit the face (flatter arches for long or oval faces, higher arches for round faces) and mentions guide lines for mapping and calipers for measuring; it gives normal brow thickness as roughly 4 to 7 mm.[17] Wikipedia likewise says practitioners consult with the client, measure the brow area and plan a symmetrical shape.[2]

The tool is a hand-held pen that carries a disposable blade made of several fine needles; reviews report needle counts from 7 to 21 and sizes around 0.16 to 0.4 mm, with finer needles giving crisper strokes. Flexible blades are described as friendlier to beginners.[17] Wikipedia says needle sets vary in number, flexibility and fineness.[2]

Wikipedia states that the most common pigments are iron-oxide based and give dark brown or black shades, and that they are sold pre-mixed for different skin tones.[2] The 2021 Indian Dermatology Online Journal review says microblading pigments are synthetic and organic, and notes that sun exposure shifts iron-oxide inks toward red and synthetic inks toward blackish-grey.[17] Anaesthesia is described in that review as mostly topical, with a numbing cream, before strokes are laid in at an angle, with main strokes running the length of the brow and supporting strokes filling gaps.[17]

The review lists variations including nano-blading with finer needles, 3D or 6D brows that vary stroke depth and flow, ombre or micro-shading done with a motorised device for a powdered look, and hybrid brows that combine manual strokes at the head with shading at the tail.[17] A Current Problems in Dermatology review also discusses combining microblading with machine-driven needle shading for background fill.[3]

A healing period follows, in which the review describes scabbing and itching as expected, with aftercare directions given by the artist and a touch-up visit after about two to three weeks to fill blank areas.[17] Wikipedia and the review both say further touch-ups are scheduled over the following year or two as pigment fades; fading depends on pigment quality, sun exposure, skin type, skincare products and medication.[2][17]

Eyebrow tattooing began as a medical procedure to cover brow loss (madarosis) and became more common for cosmetic purposes in the 1980s and 1990s in the United States and Asia, including Japan, Taiwan and Singapore. Some early practitioners were dermatologists who trained cosmetologists; early versions used a tattoo machine or a fine needle.[2]

Microblading, often called eyebrow embroidery, became popular in Singapore by about 2007 and in the US and Canada by the mid-2010s; marketing names such as 3D and 6D brows spread in the same period.[2] Reviews attribute much of its recent popularity to social media awareness.[1][17][19] A 2022 review in Current Problems in Dermatology says the method has grown quickly for cosmetic purposes and is now mature, with further refinement ahead.[3]

Reviews list microblading as a corrective option for eyebrow loss from ageing, alopecia areata or totalis, hypothyroidism, chemotherapy-induced hypotrichosis and trichotillomania.[3][17] Wikipedia also says the technique is used for thinning hairlines, a related process being hair tattooing on the scalp.[2] A 2025 review in Skin Appendage Disorders notes that eyebrows are a distinct facial feature and that any shift in their appearance affects self-perception of external beauty.[1]

Wikipedia lists misapplied pigment, migration, colour change and hyperpigmentation as common problems, with serious complications uncommon but including bloodborne infection and reactions to pigment ingredients; it says training from a comprehensive course reduces the risk of poor outcomes.[2] The 2021 review divides complications into cosmetic ones (asymmetry, unnatural shape, colour bleeding from deep deposition, fading or colour change) and functional ones (inflammation, bacterial or mycobacterial infection, herpes simplex reactivation, rare granulomas and Koebnerisation of skin disease), and attributes many problems to untrained practitioners.[17]

Case reports document delayed granulomatous reactions,[5][6] a chronic granulomatous reaction to semi-permanent eyebrow tint,[18] cutaneous sarcoidosis in a 45-year-old woman about 1.5 years after microblading,[7] Koebner phenomenon,[4] allergic contact dermatitis in a person with nickel sensitisation,[8] and preseptal cellulitis.[9] A 2023 report in the British Journal of Dermatology described mpox transmission attributed to contaminated equipment.[10] A 2022 review covers technical and clinical complications of cosmetic tattooing generally.[11] A 2025 review states that the surge in demand has gone with subjective dissatisfaction with cosmetic outcomes and an increased risk of immune-mediated adverse events.[1] The Saudi cross-sectional study of the general population examined awareness of microblading, its complications and laser removal.[19]

A 2020 pilot study in four patients with skin types III-IV reported successful removal of cosmetic eyebrow tattoos with a picosecond laser and a perfluorodecalin-infused patch.[12] A 2023 structured review of the literature identified 11 studies covering 129 patients treated for eyebrow pigment, with most using quality-switched lasers, fewer using picosecond lasers and three using carbon dioxide lasers; the authors set out to compare quality-switched and picosecond lasers.[20] A chart review of laser removal of eyeliner and eyebrow tattoos reports clinic experience.[21] The 2021 review lists conservative options such as exfoliants, laser removal with a Q-switched Nd:YAG, and colour correction as an alternative to removal, and notes laser risks including scarring and pigment change.[17]
A Current Problems in Dermatology review adds that laser removal of earlier tattoos may be indicated when a client wants a different brow style or shape for a later touch-up.[3]

In the United States the technique is not regulated at the federal level and there is no standard for testing the ink; in Canada it is treated as a personal service regulated by the provinces.[2] Practitioner licensing and hygiene rules therefore vary by jurisdiction. Wikipedia notes the equipment, pigment and process are required to be sterile.[2]

No controlled trials of the cosmetic effect were identified. The published literature is mainly reviews of the technique and its science,[1][3][17] a 2024 cross-sectional awareness study,[19] a four-patient laser-removal pilot study,[12] a structured review of laser removal,[20] and case reports of complications.[4][5][6][7][8][9][10][18]

A looksmax.org thread points to looks theorists who regard thick, dark brows as important and asks whether men have tried microblading.[14] Another thread asks about suitability for men with dark hair and light brows; the poster says most before-and-after videos looked unnatural or female-shaped, and replies range from saying the results looked better to saying the look is obviously artificial, with some suggesting minoxidil or peppermint oil instead.[15] Other threads ask whether minoxidil can be continued after microblading.[16]

The brow discussion in these communities sits alongside interest in brow ridge, eye area and hunter-eye aesthetics, in which brow density and position are treated as part of the upper-third frame; microblading is presented as the semi-permanent option, with growth products and hair transplants as other routes.[14][15]

timeline.event: Cosmetic eyebrow tattooing becomes more common in the US and Asia, after use for medical brow loss.[2]
Mainstream in Western salons around the mid-2010s; 3D and 6D brow names spread.[2]
Pilot study reports picosecond-laser removal of cosmetic eyebrow tattoos in four patients.[12]
Indian Dermatology Online Journal review 'Microblading and the Science Behind it' is published.[17]
Case reports of delayed granulomatous reactions, sarcoidosis and allergic contact dermatitis appear; a review of cosmetic tattooing complications is published.[5][6][7][8][11]
Report of mpox transmission linked to microblading; structured review of laser removal published.[10][20]
Cross-sectional study of microblading awareness and complications in Saudi Arabia published.[19]
Skin Appendage Disorders review 'Eyebrow Microblading: Science, Art, and Complications' published.[1]

lore.intro: Forum discussion treats microblading as a harder-end brow option and debates whether it looks natural on men; minoxidil and other growth approaches are discussed as alternatives.[14][15][16]

claims.claim: Microblading gives men thicker, darker brows that improve attractiveness
claims.believers: Posters cite looks theorists who value dense dark brows and ask for positive results.[14]
claims.experts: No studies of attractiveness outcomes were found; the literature is mostly on technique and complications, and a 2025 review notes brows affect self-perception.[1]

claims.believers: Some users say before-and-after examples look too perfect or female-shaped, or obviously fake.[15]
claims.experts: A review notes shape selection and pigment choice affect results, and lists unnatural shape among cosmetic complications; no studies compared male outcomes.[17]

claims.claim: Minoxidil, dermastamping and castor oil are alternatives
claims.believers: Users recommend these as growth options in place of tattoos.[15]
claims.experts: No trials of these specific regimens for brows were identified.

claims.claim: Microblading can be kept alongside minoxidil
claims.believers: Threads ask whether minoxidil can be continued after microblading.[16]
claims.experts: A review warns that exfoliants and some skincare can speed fading of pigment; no study of minoxidil with microblading was found.[17]

claims.claim: Microblading carries infection and allergy risks
claims.experts: Case reports document infection, granuloma, allergy and mpox transmission.[4][5][6][7][8][9][10]

card.summary: Semi-permanent pigment strokes tattooed into the brows; popular for fuller brows, with case reports of infection and allergy.
card.note: Literature includes granuloma, allergy, cellulitis and mpox case reports.

quick.overview:
Microblading uses a handheld blade to deposit pigment in hair-like strokes in the brows. Results fade over one to two years and need touch-ups.

Men in forums discuss it as a way to get thicker, darker brows, with mixed opinions on how natural it looks.
quick.mechanism: Pigment, usually iron-oxide based, is placed in the superficial dermis, where it stays visible until it fades.
quick.risks: Case reports describe granulomas, sarcoidosis, allergic reactions, cellulitis and mpox transmission. Regulation varies by region.

chain: Hair-like pigment strokes are drawn into the upper dermis
Sparse or patchy brows look fuller and more defined
Brow frame and eye area read as denser and more symmetrical
angle.text: Microblading fills in gaps and redraws the shape of the eyebrows with fine pigment strokes, so thin, patchy or uneven brows look denser and more symmetrical. The effect is visible immediately and fades over roughly one to two years, which is why touch-ups are part of the routine.[1][2]
